Personally I wouldn't teach OpenGL ES 3.0 or any OpenGL because its state machine (https://webgl2fundamentals.org/webgl/lessons/resources/webgl...) and horrible error system means tracking down bugs is hard. Instead I'd teach WebGPU as it's portable and has great error messaging.

I'm sure people will objected but I'd argue WebGPU is easier to understand, has better errors, has no state machine, works C++, Rust, JS/TS and other languages, and closer to modern GPU programming if you want to move to Metal or D3D12 or Vulkan later.

Further, OpenGL (and ES) are a nightmare of bugs and incompatibilities students might run into that WebGPU fixes.

That said, the article mentions Apple platforms where you can use ANGLE if you happened to have students stuck there.

I mostly agree regarding GL's programming model, but tbf some problems have been fixed by WebGL2 (much better validation and error reporting - e.g. very helpful error messages right on the browser console - and it's probably the least buggy and most portable 3D API implementation of them all, including the current state of WebGPU.

For teaching I would generally use the web browser via WebGL2 or WebGPU, just because those APIs require much less boilerplate in the browser environment to get to your first triangle and the edit-test-loop is pretty much instant.

In real life there’s lots of bugs around and difficult to read error messages.

Re. the boilerplate just have students clone a pre-fabbed repo with the boilerplate handled for them.

The real question should be whether you want students to know how to program in a low programming language or not. Whether they should see what the reality of programming is or not.

If they can’t program in C/C++ and debug the error messages how are they going to survive in the wild? I guess they’ll use an LLM.

> If they can’t program in C/C++ and debug the error messages how are they going to survive in the wild?

The problem is that you don't get *any* error messages from native GL in the first place (unless you wire up a debug-message callback via the optional KHR_debug extension which isn't available everywhere), and the builtin error system via glGetError() is pretty much completely useless.

Other APIs don't suffer from this problem, D3D, Vulkan and Metal all have excellent validation layers which give very helpful messages, and WebGL or WebGPU running in browsers basically implement such a validation layer out of the box.

small nit, that's not true, since GL4.3 the modern debug message callback is core so you can rely on it. Sure that won't save you on MacOS but if you can target modern OpenGL this isn't a problem in practice

"unless you wire up a debug-message callback via the optional KHR_debug extension which isn't available everywhere"

The beauty of OpenGL versus say Direct3D is that OpenGL is extensible and thus you can add that feature should you so choose.
Fortunately "beauty lies in the eye of the beholder" ;) I definitely prefer the D3D model instead of the extension soup of GL or Vulkan.
The KHR_debug is also kind of a pain to use because it gets called asynchronously (which is what you want, yes, but the difficulty is still there).

WebGPU will however always suffer from being an API designed for the Web, and targeting 2015 thereabouts hardware.

Better than OpenGL, but don't expect that much improvements coming into their way, other than what the Chrome team might feel like pushing, as I doubt Firefox or Safari teams have much left to say about where it goes beyond version 1.0.

> but don't expect that much improvements

What improvements are needed? It sees pretty much complete to me and I think it's a good thing for it to be in maintenance mode (ie stable).

The rigid resource binding model via BindGroup objects in WebGPU is already outdated (and funny enough, an area where WebGPU is actually slower than WebGL2, at least when assuming that bindings need to change frequently and unpredictably).

This was a restriction of the Vulkan 1.0 API and modelling the WebGPU resource binding model around that was a quite predictable problem. It would have been better to come up with a slim abstraction that might cost some performance on Vulkan (which is only really relevant on Android phones and Linux desktops), but at least would not slow down WebGPU across all platforms.

And now even the Vulkan maintainers have realized the problem and are introducing the much more flexible descriptor-heap extension (about a decade late, but better late than never).

WebGPU is essentially the frozen cross-section of 3D APIs from about a decade ago, and the state of GPU hardware from about 15 to 20 years ago (but tbf, apart from the broken binding model there wasn't much that could be done, because most restrictions are coming from mobile GPUs which a browser 3D API simply must support).

1. monolithic pipelines, pretty much no hardware works like that, the hash-and-cache design makes your design inflexible and adds a ton of overhead

2. WGSL, like come on

3. Hilariously outdated feature set, no mesh shaders, no HWRT, cooperative matrices/tensors, etc.

4. It's security-focused because web untrusted code:tm: so most of the calls are hilariously slow. Yes even the desktop implementations. There's no good webGPU implementation out there

5. it's also not simple to either implement or use. it's basically vulkan's difficulty without any of the advantages....

I have never understood and will never understand why so many programming luminaries fell in love with OpenGL. It violates the most important engineering precept that I try to follow when I design a library: minimize hidden state. OpenGL is nothing but hidden state. You have no way to tell what a piece of code is going to render without seeing everything that set up the internal stack beforehand, perhaps thousands of lines away, or in entirely different modules that you might not even have access to.

I won’t defend the state soup, but there are upsides: the GL api has no structs which makes it easier to port the API to different languages and environments.

The state model isn’t nearly as much of an issue for the fixed function architectures it was originally developed for, you can see how adherence to the extension mechanism and the resulting design by committee left its marks. Microsoft didn’t have those constraints.

At least partly, it’s a form of choice-supportive bias (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choice-supportive_bias).

Your mind cannot live with the idea that you spent many, many hours learning an ugly API, so it makes you think it is better than it is.
Sounds like C++ and OpenGL are BFFs.

The quip is that C++ is fool's gold; Flying around in code and getting all the little mechanical details right really feels like getting things done. (It's just wizard- or mastery-flavored busywork. Glitter.)

I've later come to suspect that this glittering is sometimes useful as… fuel? Feeling-of-progress hands-on motivation-fuel.

My take is that older versions of GL feel nicer to teach to beginner programmers because they have so many specific functions to do each specific thing. You can have a lot of verbose, step-by-step instruction. But, much of what you have to convey is understanding of a convoluted interface to a hidden state machine. And, the one-step-at-a-time nature of the old interfaces build bad habits that don’t scale when you get serious.

With 4.6 we can get Direct State Access, Programmable Vertex Pulling and MultidrawIndirect. With that we can move the complexity from “lots of functions to manipulate a state machine” to a few functions that strongly resemble using malloc and memcpy to work with arrays of structs. That’s not trivial. But, it should be extremely familiar. It’s visible, flexible, scalable, and it sets you up to move on to Vulkan after you’ve learned the essentials of 3D rendering.

OpenGL with it's combination of hand-holding and relative simplicity as compared to Vulkan and limits of a predefined shader pipeline as compared to a pure software implementation is exactly the thing that I needed to get into graphics programming. Nice breakdown. I've been wondering why it's so complicated to program on the GPU compared to the CPU. Is it a language paradigm issue or maybe a hardware design limitation? I always think of this when looking at the graphic APIs, espeically Vulkan.

It's mostly hardware design limitations. GPU hardware is way more diverse than CPU hardware, so you need to distribute shaders as either source code or a portable intermediate representation, in both cases compiled at runtime for the user's actual GPU. There are also many fixed function parts of the graphics pipeline with wildly different behavior on different hardware which you need to abstract over. And it all runs in parallel with the CPU, often with a separate pool of RAM, so you need implicit or explicit synchronization and data transfer which adds a lot of complexity especially in error cases.

If you really want to see why all the cruft is there, and how much you could remove if you dropped support for older hardware, look no further than Sebastian Aaltonen's "No Graphics API" blog post (which he actually implemented too): https://www.sebastianaaltonen.com/blog/no-graphics-api/

I think most of it comes down to 'historical accidents' tbh.

E.g. if CPUs would have closed ISAs and heavily guarded IPs, you'd also need a 'driver' and an 'OpenCPU API' to make any use of them (of course the public ISA of a CPU is essentially the driver interface baked into the hardware).

The other big difference is focus on decent single-thread performance for CPUs versus performing thousands of small tasks in parallel on GPUs, but each one slowly. This difference causes a different programming model (e.g. running an entire application in a single 'main' function from start to finish, versus spawning small specialized tasks which are running across hundreds of threads).

And the specific problem with Vulkan is that it tried to solve two conflicting requirements: on one hand being an explicit low-level API without 'magic abstractions', on the other hand supporting very different GPU architectures (especially the mobile GPU zoo). The resulting mess was quite predictable to be honest...

You underestimate the effect of two factors.

First, GPUs aren't simply "highly parallel CPUs", they also contain a whole lot of fixed function hardware that is specialized for real-time computer graphics. This hardware isn't exposed as "fancy instructions", it is set up in other ways, which is achieved through a device driver.

Second: GPUs are coprocessor, separate from the CPU where another OS is running. This also necessitates a device driver to manage scheduling, synchronization, etc. with the main OS. Because, in case you were not aware, the GPU itself runs its own little operating system, although it is rarely called that.

> they also contain a whole lot of fixed function hardware that is specialized for real-time computer graphics. This hardware isn't exposed as "fancy instructions", it is set up in other ways, which is achieved through a device driver.

Those hardwired fixed-function parts are getting fewer and less important though (ok, and then raytracing units entered the scene...). Also AFAIK something like a texture sampling operation is indeed a 'fancy instruction'(?), even though the actual texture sampling is done by a 'fixed function' hardware unit.

> This also necessitates a device driver to manage scheduling, synchronization, etc. with the main OS.

I bet this type of GPU/CPU handshaking work could also be baked into the hardware (similar to CPU mirocode) and exposed via a standardized memory mapped IO interface (or whatever the current mechanism is for letting the CPU control the GPU). E.g. a CPU also implements similar protocols to talk to the rest of the computer system (e.g. memory and other CPUs), but this is mainly implemented as "hardware protocols" - drivers "just" offer more flexibility for hardware vendors because they can delegate the standardization into software.

...also a lot of the "CPU / GPU software ecosystem" was probably shaped by CPU and GPU vendors historically being different companies, and once the big consolidation started, the conventions were already set in stone.

> Those hardwired fixed-function parts are getting fewer and less important though

There is more machinery internally than what the user can see. Even "low level" APIs hide quite a lot of the internal complexity.

> Also AFAIK something like a texture sampling operation is indeed a 'fancy instruction'(?)

Yes, and no. The "I want to sample this texture" part looks like a fancy instruction to the shader processor. But there is a fair amount of setup that needs to be done before and after, and that is the responsibility of the device driver. Stuff like: where is the data, how is it arranged in memory, how it is to be sampled, etc.

As you point out, the texture units are coprocessors inside the coprocessor that is the GPU itself. It is turtles all the way down. Think of a GPU as a whole network of processors inside a chip, some of which are hidden from the application programmer.

> I bet this type of GPU/CPU handshaking work could also be baked into the hardware (similar to CPU mirocode) and exposed via a standardized memory mapped IO interface (or whatever the current mechanism is for letting the CPU control the GPU)

Attempts have been made. Last time I checked, they had not been very successful, but I have not kept up with the latest developments after retirement.

The way this normally works is that there is a circular command buffer where the CPU inserts commands and the GPU consumes them. It works; there is nothing wrong with it. It is the obvious way to handle asynchronous coprocessors.

> E.g. a CPU also implements similar protocols to talk to the rest of the computer system (e.g. memory and other CPUs), but this is mainly implemented as "hardware protocols" - drivers "just" offer more flexibility for hardware vendors because they can delegate the standardization into software.

I suspect you underestimate the amount of setup that is necessary to drive a GPU. And the amount of asynchronous resource management involved.

Let me put it this other way: the people doing this for a living for decades know what they are doing. There have been attempts to try to make GPUs that behave more like CPUs in terms of how they are driven, and they have not been very successful so far, to my knowledge. AMD acquired ATI back in 2006, so it is not like there hasn't been enough time for the concept to cook in the oven. See also Intel's Larrabee.

part of the reason is historical cruft & history path dependency. GPUs didn't start as general computing device for parallelism but a device for the specific purpose of accelerating graphics with very specific fixed functions for that job and only that. with time that fixed pipeline became more complex and more configurable, not fixed/more flexible and hacks were in parallel used to make use of it for tasks outside graphics those hacks were later made into something more formal (CUDA/OpenCL).

CUDA being the winner (closed source, not really usable on non-nvidia GPUs) between those 2 and nvidia not wanting to open their competitive advantage to the competition for the niche of non gamings uses / scientific computing (and later AI, which became a huge win for nvidia).

vulkan came around after as this open thing (based on a previous attempt by AMD called mantle) that's trying to break down the leaky abstractions and the divide between language for graphics & video games and separate language/frameworks for gpu non-graphic computing with the promise of giving more control and more room for squeezing performance from the hardware at the cost of more complexity with the idea that you'll probably build your own abstractions on top of it for your subset of applications.

> If GPU were from the get go designed as a parallelism tool first and video game tools second the hardware architecture and the language would probably be different than today and simpler (and if the competition between the duopoly didn't sabotage things)

> If GPU were from the get go designed as a parallelism tool first and video game tools second the hardware architecture and the language would probably be different than today and simpler (...)

The market demand was for video game tools, though.

People didn't wanted faster compute, they wanted their computer games to work smoothly on the hardware they already own. Therefore, they preferred to spend 100-200€ on a point upgrade, much like RAM, than scrapping their 2k€ PC.

One thing that helped me understand it was to reframe it as a network application, where you have a client running on the CPU and a server running on the GPU (the shaders).

A bunch of the complexity comes from having to write both client and server, and the communication protocol between them, then some more comes from the client being responsible for spinning up the server. As with every network service, client/server traffic is the slowest part of the architecture, so a bunch of complexity then comes from having to minimise the amount of network calls (or draw calls, in this case).

Then you hit the part where all of this is performance critical (soft-realtime requirements), so the whole thing is geared towards “writing your own userspace IP stack in C++” rather than “writing a flask application in Python”.

The thing that makes it "hard" is that it's all indirect. You compile a program for the GPU (a shader). Then you have to setup data (textures and buffers) for it. Then, you need to spend a bunch of time telling the GPU how to use that data, offsets where each piece of data is, what formats the data is in,, how to advance to the next piece of data, etc.. etc..

There are a few libraries that try to abstract over all this indirection but all the graphics APIs themselves are lower-level so you're left to do all of that yourself.

https://docs.swmansion.com/TypeGPU/

https://github.com/google/toucan

If you care about every last bit of performance, CPUs are difficult to program for as well, possibly more difficult than a GPU.

Generally GPUs punish you more by bad performance if you don't optimise your code.

It's not more complicated, you have things like CUDA which is basically C/C++ that compiles to GPU.

But GPUs have thousands of cores, which means if you want any benefit, the smallest data type you must use is something like array[n * 1024], or your GPU is wasted doing nothing. So you must shape your programs into that memory model or you're just wasting your time (and GPU).

That's >50% of the problem.
Right, that makes sense. There's a ton of overhead in the setup though, I'm assuming that's because everything runs on the CPU by default. Is this then an OS design choice? Thanks for your input.

There can be overhead, though GPU memory + drivers are some of the most optimized software in the world.

Some OS/hardware have separate GPU memory (Nvidia), some have unified memory (Macos, modern consoles), but moving memory is usually not the problem.

Things don't "run on CPU by default", it's up to the programmer where to run it. But the CPU and GPU paradigm of "running a program" are very different, since on GPU you're running SIMD (i.e. running your code on arrays) or else there is no point to use a GPU.
For me, if-branching is the hardest to wrap my head around. "If"s are so natural to CPU programming that it's second nature to any developer but on GPU, it's expensive.

instead of iterating over an array and if-branching to one of two paths for each item, conceive of your conditionals as logic operations which test for set membership (i.e. "is this array item a member of the set i care about?") and with this array mask of "do the thing or don't do the thing" flags, you can mutate your data 0 or 1 times.

the key for me is thinking in terms of sets—much of your conditional logic is probably about sorting things into sets anyway.

Vulkan, OpenGL and DirectX make GPU programming more difficult than it has to be for multiple reasons, some of which other people here have mentioned. They are also low level, focused on high performance, and are primarily designed and written for game engines. Making them easy to learn for newcomers is pretty low on the priority list. ShaderToy makes it easy by taking care of everything except the GLSL, you might like it. You can also try CUDA, which is generally a lot easier than Vulkan. For a really easy/fun time with CUDA, try Warp - it’s CUDA in Python.

It's partially historical; I'm sure if we redesigned GPGPU today from the ground up, we'd have an entirely different pipeline. And partially due to hardware vendor lock-in; you can't really design an alternative to Vulkan/d3d12 even if you had the skill and drive to do so.

But also partly in the fact that the GPU is specialized for certain operations over a CPU. It wants and need to obtain data in a different way from a CPU to maximize throughput. So language constructs are designed around making sure developers stay on this fast path. The complexity can be seen as some intentional gatekeeping to signal that this kind of programming is only for specific kinds of problems.

That middle ground is often called DirectX 11 but sadly it's stuck to a specific platform.

dx11 isn't bad but it has a looot of cruft around it, writing a good constant buffer manager is witchcraft (remember, there's no "loose uniforms" injected into the command stream, it's all constant buffer updates, drivers do all sorts of writecombining magic to mitigate it, but the naive map / unmap cycle without any driver optimisations would absolutely tank....

Look at a GDC talk (https://d29g4g2dyqv443.cloudfront.net/sites/default/files/ak...), efficient dx11 is also "reinvent a diy memory allocator" level except that you don't have much control.

btw you can run dx11 on other platforms because dxvk exists, but while d3d9vk is a solid idea (high-level API, lowering to vulkan often makes it much faster than the crummy MS d3d9 runtime + DDI combo), d3d11vk is just often a wash or even a regression. I've had to debug dxvk-only perf problems a bit too many times...

anyway, point is, it's not really an easy-to-use or intuitive API

> writing a good constant buffer manager is witchcraft

Tbh, I think the main lesson is simply to not try to work around the specific 3D API conventions too much, e.g. don't try to shoehorn mechanisms into the D3D11 layer that would be straightforward in Vulkan or D3D12 but would disable the special fast-paths in D3D11.

E.g. for a traditional "one uniform update per draw call" loop with one small constant buffer per shader updated via plain old UpdateSubresource(), D3D11 is incredibly fast (you can easily do hundreds-of-thousands update+drawcall pairs like this per 60Hz frame on a somewhat recent - e.g. post-2016 or so - mid-level gaming PC.

Of course trying to emulate D3D11 on Vulkan or D3D12 might have all sorts of issues that don't exist on a good "native" D3D11 driver.

Also somewhat related: in a GL shim it's typically still faster to update uniform data via the old glUniform*v calls instead of using uniform buffers, apparently most GL drivers lack the special fast-path optimizations of small D3D11 constant buffers, and the more abstract glUniform calls seems to give the driver more 'wiggle room' to implement an optimal upload path.

I mean sure you can do a generic layer and common denominator stuff, basically the kinda stuff webgpu or those rendering abstractions do and that's fair enough, it works well for simpler stuff!

The problem really is that if you do that you'll end up with random weird stalls or perf problems you can't really debug sadly :\

Re GL ye glUniform is usually much faster because you just do a lot less, you're writing a small amount of data directly into constant memory, it doesn't need resource tracking. UBOs / constant buffers come back to the theoretically slow but can-be-made-faster-with-driver-heuristics approach...i.e. if you see a small UBO which is only used as a UBO, you get the same direct constant bank upload

On NV it's quite fast, on AMD it's not really optimised, on intel just use buffersubdata because everything else sucks....

Nothing is an easy to use intuitive api with all the features and all the performance, it's (Dx11) the sweet spot of where I felt like it was easy to learn and easy to use without worrying about performance too much.

Sure if you are building the newer rendering pipelines DirectX 11 leaves a lot on the table but it brought a lot of nice things with it, Debug Runtime alone was worth moving to it, 99/100 times your app written in DirectX 11 even if not optimised properly will perform better than DirectX 9 in my experience.

This holds with OpenGL though the modern OpenGL 4.6 and stuff wasn't bad, but it's a lot of cruft still.

Either way there are no perfect APIs, a truly general purpose API that just gives you basics like Texture handling and io and data mapping would be enough today imho. Fully general purpose compute APIs are the solution with some additional tweaks to make graphics stuff convenient. IMHO

Though it's definitely much harder than plain and simple paint colors and textures on vertices & geometry uv approach of old.
